Subject: Embeddings integration: batching & normalization — post-call recap

Hi Michael / Anna — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our call + proposed next steps so we stay aligned.

What we heard:
- You already have embeddings in production with ProviderX (1536-dim, float32).
- Primary uses: semantic search for customer support articles + a reranker for QA results.
- Pain points: high per-vector cost, inconsistent similarity scores after migration attempts, and latency spikes during bulk upserts.

Redwood recommendations (high level):
1) Vector size and model: 1536 dims is reasonable to retain if you need parity; we also recommend evaluating 1024-dim variants for cost/latency tradeoffs (few percent AUC drop in some tasks).
2) Batching & upsert strategy: use incremental upserts + 5-10k vector batching for bulk migrations to minimize API overhead. For real-time ingestion, target 128-512 vectors per batch depending on your latency SLO.
3) Normalization: normalize to unit vectors (L2) on ingest to keep cosine similarity stable across providers.
4) Reranker integration: keep a two-stage pipeline — cheap ANN recall on normalized embeddings, then model-based reranker (semantic scoring or instruction-tuned LM).

Attached: a short migration plan and example batching config (redwood-embeddings-migration-plan.pdf, kv-batching-config.yaml).

Immediate next steps:
- Rishi: will send a short technical note with suggested batch sizes, indexing options, and sample SDK calls (by EOD tomorrow).
- FinServ: confirm whether you need documented parity (identical dims/metric) or are open to dimension reduction for cost.
- Marissa/Vivek: propose a follow-up technical working session with your infra + data team next week.

If that looks good I'll schedule the session.

Hey Michael / Anna — quick technical follow-up to the questions Michael raised. TL;DR: server-side normalization + staged backfill with dual-index routing is what we recommend.

1) Dimensionality and thresholds:
- If you keep 1536 dims and normalize (L2), your existing cosine thresholds should be ~directly comparable. We usually see <1-3% shift after moving providers when normalization and metric (cosine) are identical.
- Moving to 1024 dims typically reduces compute and storage ~20-30%; similarity thresholds can shift depending on your dataset. We recommend running a small A/B evaluation on a held-out set (5-10k queries) to measure true delta.

2) Bulk migration strategy (recommended):
- Stage 0: Create a new index in Redwood-managed vector store.
- Stage 1: Backfill in batches of 5k vectors (recommended). Backfill uses low-priority worker nodes to avoid contention.
- Stage 2: Dual-index routing (read from both ProviderX and Redwood) for a short sanity window; serve 100% from ProviderX until backfill passes consistency checks, then switch traffic to Redwood index. This avoids degraded results during migration.

3) Server-side normalization:
- Yes — Redwood supports server-side L2 normalization on ingest. We can also accept already-normalized vectors; we detect and skip double-normalization if input vectors are already unit-length.

4) ANN behavior differences:
- Redwood default index (HNSW-configured) biases for lower memory footprint and predictable per-query latency under load. ProviderX default may use different ef/search tuning; we can surface ef/search params in the migration plan so you can mirror behavior during evaluation.

5) SDK & auth snippets (short):
- SDK pseudo:
  from redwood import EmbeddingsClient
  client = EmbeddingsClient(api_key="REDACTED")
  vectors = client.embed_batch(doc_texts, model="rw-emb-1536")
  client.upsert("finserv-index", vectors, normalize=True, batch_size=5000)

6) Monitoring hooks:
- We'll provide logs for upsert success/failure counts, per-batch latency, and a migration consistency report comparing a sample of embeddings between ProviderX and Redwood.

I'll attach a short snippet of recommended HNSW params and a sample backfill script to the working doc. Happy to discuss in the tech session.
